The histogram above shows how many values from a dataset fall into each group. What is the modal group of the dataset?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
When data is grouped into intervals, the modal group is the group with the highest frequency.

From a histogram, we can directly compare the bar heights to see how often values from each group occurs.

In our case, the tallest bar corresponds to the group [MATH: 9-14,] which has a frequency of [MATH: 12,] more than any other group.

Therefore, the modal group of the dataset is [MATH: 9-14.]

A teacher recorded students' test scores in a test. The histogram above shows how many students achieved each score. What was the median score?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To find the median from a histogram, we first convert the histogram into a frequency table.

On a histogram, the horizontal axis shows the values in the dataset, and the vertical axis tells us how many times each value appears.

In our case, we build the frequency table below and compute cumulative frequencies.

Score

Students

Cumulative Frequency

[MATH: 76]

[MATH: 3]

[MATH: 3]

[MATH: 77]

[MATH: 5]

[MATH: 8]

[MATH: 78]

[MATH: 7]

[MATH: 15]

[MATH: 79]

[MATH: 3]

[MATH: 18]

[MATH: 80]

[MATH: 2]

[MATH: 20]

Thus, the total number of values is [MATH: N = 3 + 5 + 7 + 3 + 2 = 20.] Since this is an even number, the median is the average of the values in the following positions: [MATH: \dfrac{N}{2} = \dfrac{20}{2} = 10\textrm{th} \qquad \text{and} \qquad 10 + 1 = 11\textrm{th}]

Looking at the cumulative frequency column in our table, we see the following:

  • Up to the second row, the table covers [MATH: 8] positions in total.

  • Up to the third row, the table covers [MATH: 15] positions in total.

So, the [MATH: 10]th and [MATH: 11]th positions both fall in the third row and correspond to the value [MATH: 78.] Therefore, the median is [MATH: Median|= (78 + 78)/(2); = (156)/(2); = 78points.]

Content:
When grouped data is displayed in a histogram, we can only estimate the median. This is because we don't know the exact values that make up our data set.

Content:
To estimate the median in such cases, we create a cumulative frequency table as before, and then find the group in which the median lies.

Content:
Let’s see how this works with an example. In which group does the median of the following dataset lie?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c70ecb5823a5325b265bbed877bee015]

Content:
The cumulative frequency table corresponding to this histogram is as follows:

Content:
| Value | Frequency | Cumulative Frequency |
| [MATH: 9-12] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: 12-15] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] |
| [MATH: 15-18] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 6] |
| [MATH: 18-21] | [MATH: 6] | [MATH: 12] |
| [MATH: 21-24] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 17] |

Content:
Thus, the total number of values is

Content:
[MATH: 1+2+3+6+5=17.]
Since [MATH: 17] is an odd number, the median is in the following position:
[MATH: \dfrac{17+1}{2}=\dfrac{18}{2}=9\textrm{th}]

Content:
Now we determine where the [MATH: 9]th value falls. Looking at the cumulative frequency column in our table, we see the following:

Content:
- Up to the third row, the table covers [MATH: 6] positions in total.
- Up to the fourth row, the table covers [MATH: 12] positions in total.

Content:
Therefore, the [MATH: 9]th value falls in the fourth interval, which is
[MATH: 18-21.]

Content:
So, the true median lies somewhere between [MATH: 18] and [MATH: 21.]

[MATH: \dfrac{20}{2} = 10 \qquad \text{and} \qquad 10 + 1 = 11.]

Now we determine where the [MATH: 10]th and [MATH: 11]th values fall. Looking at the cumulative frequency column in our table, we see the following:

  • Up to the second row, the table covers [MATH: 10] positions in total.

  • Up to the third row, the table covers [MATH: 13] positions in total.

So, we have that

  • the [MATH: 10]th value falls in the second row corresponding to the group [MATH: 15-18,] while

  • the [MATH: 11]th value falls in the third row corresponding to the group [MATH: 18-21.]

The median could fall in either of these groups. Of the given options:

  • Option I, [MATH: 17.5,] falls within the group [MATH: 15-18,] so could be the median.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to determine the mean, median, and mode from a histogram.

Content:
Let's begin with the mode. For example, what is the mode of the dataset represented by the histogram below?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b5d89594c394d265ddb81e63e68e80e8]

Content:
The mode is the value or values that appear most frequently in a dataset.

Content:
From a histogram, we can directly compare the heights of each bar to see how often each value occurs.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/105e14d9f79f6fe46313f25b58478098]

Content:
In this case, the tallest bars correspond to the values [MATH: 18] and [MATH: 21,] which both appear in the dataset [MATH: 8] times. Since both of these values occur most frequently and with equal frequency, the dataset is bimodal (i.e., it has two modes). Therefore, the modes are [MATH: 18] and [MATH: 21.]

Content:
Let's now examine an example involving grouped data.

---

Item 2 — Example: Determining Modes From Histograms

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/bfee0e608778e5efdf98f916b731f0a0]

The histogram above shows how many values from a dataset fall into each group. What is the modal group of the dataset?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
When data is grouped into intervals, the modal group is the group with the highest frequency.

From a histogram, we can directly compare the bar heights to see how often values from each group occurs.

[IMG: /graphics/97aefa3051ac31f529496e4682341a17]

In our case, the tallest bar corresponds to the group [MATH: 9-14,] which has a frequency of [MATH: 12,] more than any other group.

Therefore, the modal group of the dataset is [MATH: 9-14.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Calculating Medians

Content:
What is the median of the dataset given by the histogram below?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c702dfdd0564a1ab389cf0f658613838]

Content:
To find the median from a histogram, we first convert the histogram into a cumulative frequency table.

Content:
In our case, the cumulative frequency table corresponding to this histogram is given below.

Content:
| Value | Frequency | Cumulative Frequency |
| [MATH: 0.8] | [MATH: 6] | [MATH: 6] |
| [MATH: 1.0] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 9] |
| [MATH: 1.2] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 14] |
| [MATH: 1.4] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 15] |

Content:
Thus, the total number of values in our data set equals [MATH: 15.] Since this is an odd number, the median is the value in the following position:

Content:
[MATH: (15 + 1)/(2) = (16)/(2) = 8th]

Content:
Now we determine where the [MATH: 8]th value falls. Looking at the cumulative frequency column in our table, we see the following:

Content:
- The first row of the table covers the first [MATH: 6] positions.
- Up to the second row, the table covers [MATH: 9] positions in total.

Content:
So, the [MATH: 8]th value falls in the second row and corresponds to the value [MATH: 1.0.] Therefore, the median is

Content:
[MATH: Median = 1.0]

---

Item 6 — Example: Calculating Medians From Histograms

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/137e5ca2c2005cbc756616b4d5698824]

A teacher recorded students' test scores in a test. The histogram above shows how many students achieved each score. What was the median score?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To find the median from a histogram, we first convert the histogram into a frequency table.

On a histogram, the horizontal axis shows the values in the dataset, and the vertical axis tells us how many times each value appears.

In our case, we build the frequency table below and compute cumulative frequencies.

| Score | Students | Cumulative Frequency |
| [MATH: 76] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 3] |
| [MATH: 77] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 8] |
| [MATH: 78] | [MATH: 7] | [MATH: 15] |
| [MATH: 79] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 18] |
| [MATH: 80] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 20] |

Thus, the total number of values is
[MATH: N = 3 + 5 + 7 + 3 + 2 = 20.]
Since this is an even number, the median is the average of the values in the following positions:
[MATH: \dfrac{N}{2} = \dfrac{20}{2} = 10\textrm{th}
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
10 + 1 = 11\textrm{th}]

Looking at the cumulative frequency column in our table, we see the following:

- Up to the second row, the table covers [MATH: 8] positions in total.
- Up to the third row, the table covers [MATH: 15] positions in total.

So, the [MATH: 10]th and [MATH: 11]th positions both fall in the third row and correspond to the value [MATH: 78.] Therefore, the median is
[MATH: Median|= (78 + 78)/(2); = (156)/(2); = 78points.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Estimating Medians When the Data Is Grouped

Content:
When grouped data is displayed in a histogram, we can only estimate the median. This is because we don't know the exact values that make up our data set.

Content:
To estimate the median in such cases, we create a cumulative frequency table as before, and then find the group in which the median lies.

Content:
Let’s see how this works with an example. In which group does the median of the following dataset lie?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c70ecb5823a5325b265bbed877bee015]

Content:
The cumulative frequency table corresponding to this histogram is as follows:

| Value | Frequency | Cumulative Frequency |
| [MATH: 9-12] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: 12-15] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] |
| [MATH: 15-18] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 6] |
| [MATH: 18-21] | [MATH: 6] | [MATH: 12] |
| [MATH: 21-24] | [MATH: 5] | [MATH: 17] |

Content:
Thus, the total number of values is

Content:
[MATH: 1+2+3+6+5=17.]
Since [MATH: 17] is an odd number, the median is in the following position:
[MATH: \dfrac{17+1}{2}=\dfrac{18}{2}=9\textrm{th}]

Content:
Now we determine where the [MATH: 9]th value falls. Looking at the cumulative frequency column in our table, we see the following:

Content:
- Up to the third row, the table covers [MATH: 6] positions in total.
- Up to the fourth row, the table covers [MATH: 12] positions in total.

Content:
Therefore, the [MATH: 9]th value falls in the fourth interval, which is
[MATH: 18-21.]

Content:
So, the true median lies somewhere between [MATH: 18] and [MATH: 21.]
